story.title: Senate Confirms Todd Blanche as Attorney General in Narrow Vote
story.summary: The U.S. Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as Attorney General with a narrow 50-49 vote early Saturday morning. Blanche, a former personal lawyer for President Trump, received crucial support from Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who was the deciding vote in a contentious confirmation process. Concerns regarding the independence of the office were raised during the proceedings.

event_overview.title: About Sen. Cassidy Supports Todd Blanche's Attorney General Confirmation
event_overview.subject: Sen. Cassidy Supports Todd Blanche's Attorney General Confirmation
event_overview.summary: This event concerns President Donald Trump’s 2026 nomination of Todd Blanche to become U.S. attorney general, after Blanche had served as deputy attorney general and then acting attorney general. The nomination went through Senate Judiciary Committee hearings in July before the Senate confirmed him on August 8, 2026, following closely watched support from Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana.

facts.label: Nomination and office
facts.value: President Trump sent Blanche’s nomination to the Senate on June 8, 2026, to serve as attorney general, the head of the Department of Justice and the federal government’s chief law-enforcement officer.

facts.label: Senate’s role
facts.value: The Constitution assigns the Senate the role of considering and confirming presidential executive nominations; the Senate Judiciary Committee conducted Blanche’s confirmation hearings on July 15 and 16, 2026, in the Hart Senate Office Building.

facts.label: Prior Justice Department role
facts.value: Blanche was confirmed as deputy attorney general on March 5, 2025, by a 52–46 Senate vote. The deputy attorney general is the department’s second-ranking official and may exercise much of the attorney general’s authority.

facts.label: Acting attorney general service
facts.value: Blanche became acting attorney general on April 2, 2026, replacing Pamela Bondi; he remained the administration’s nominee for the permanent post during the Senate process.

facts.label: Confirmation outcome
facts.value: The Senate confirmed Blanche on August 8, 2026, after Cassidy announced his support the previous day; reporting characterized the vote as narrow.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers Cassidy’s late support and the final Senate confirmation, not the full nomination process, hearing record, or Blanche’s broader Justice Department actions.

explore_lenses.label: What changed beyond Blanche's acting role?
explore_lenses.title: Senate consent moves DOJ beyond an acting chief
explore_lenses.summary: The 50-49 vote gives the Senate's advice and consent for Todd Blanche to lead the Justice Department, replacing the temporary arrangement under which he had been acting attorney general. It does not itself establish a new policy agenda or resolve concerns about how independently he will use the office.

claims.text: The Senate confirmed Blanche 50-49 early on August 8, 2026; reporting says he had led the department in an acting capacity after Pam Bondi was fired in April.
Federal law provides that the attorney general is appointed by the president with Senate advice and consent and is the head of the Justice Department.
The attorney general holds the department's functions except for specified statutory exceptions, making the office central to DOJ-wide direction rather than limited to a single portfolio.

explore_lenses.label: Why did Cassidy back him while others opposed?
explore_lenses.title: A decisive Republican vote followed written concessions
explore_lenses.summary: Bill Cassidy's support supplied the margin after two Republican senators announced opposition. Supporters cited Blanche's record and the practical question of whom Trump might nominate instead; critics focused on whether the Justice Department could remain independent of the White House.

claims.text: Cassidy was described as the decisive vote and said he believed Blanche was the best option President Trump would put forward.
Lisa Murkowski joined Susan Collins in opposing the nomination; Murkowski said the country needed an attorney general who would check the administration's worst impulses.

During the confirmation fight, Blanche made written commitments to abandon a proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund for Trump allies and narrow a tax-related arrangement involving Trump and his family.
Blanche has defended his tenure by saying the department reduced crime and corrected what he characterizes as wrongs committed against Trump and conservative allies by the prior administration.

explore_lenses.label: What powers and constraints matter now?
explore_lenses.title: The confirmation ends one hurdle, not oversight
explore_lenses.summary: As attorney general, Blanche will direct the Justice Department's functions and can make consequential management and enforcement decisions. But his decisions remain subject to statutory limits, court review where applicable, congressional oversight, and internal DOJ rules; confirmation does not settle disputes over independence.

claims.text: The Justice Department statute vests the department's functions in the attorney general, subject to listed exceptions, and authorizes the attorney general to appoint officials to detect and prosecute federal crimes.

Before confirmation, the vacancy statute allowed the deputy attorney general to exercise the attorney general's duties during a vacancy, absence, or disability; Blanche's confirmation removes the need to rely on that acting-official arrangement for him to lead DOJ.
Critics' central concern is prospective: whether Blanche will act independently when Trump seeks investigations or policies affecting political allies or opponents.

story_report.summary: The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general in a 50-49 vote early Aug. 8, installing President Trump’s former personal lawyer as the Justice Department’s Senate-confirmed leader after he had been serving in an acting capacity. The result gives Blanche formal authority over a department whose functions are generally vested in the attorney general, while leaving open questions about how he will exercise that authority and maintain independence from the administration.

sections.heading: Attorney General Authority at Justice Department
sections.body: Federal law provides that the attorney general is appointed by the president with the Senate’s advice and consent and serves as head of the Justice Department. The office holds the department’s functions except where statutes specify otherwise, and the attorney general may appoint officials to detect and prosecute federal crimes. Before Blanche’s confirmation, vacancy law allowed the deputy attorney general to perform the attorney general’s duties during a vacancy, absence or disability.

sections.heading: Cassidy Support and Independence Concerns
sections.body: Sen. Bill Cassidy was described as the decisive vote and said he believed Blanche was the best option Trump would put forward. Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins opposed the nomination; Murkowski said the country needed an attorney general who would check the administration’s worst impulses. During the confirmation fight, Blanche made written commitments to abandon a proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund for Trump allies and narrow a tax-related arrangement involving Trump and his family.

unresolved.text: The reviewed sources do not establish when Blanche will take the oath of office or identify immediate personnel, investigative or policy decisions following his confirmation.

It remains unresolved whether Blanche’s written commitments are legally enforceable, whether similar initiatives could proceed through other mechanisms, and whether his future actions will test concerns about independence from Trump.

related_stories.title: Court Halts Trump's White House Ballroom Construction, Appeals Expected
related_stories.summary: A federal appeals court has ordered the halt of construction on Donald Trump's planned $400 million ballroom at the White House, stating that such a significant alteration requires congressional approval. The ruling follows a challenge from the National Trust for Historic Preservation and is seen as a test of presidential power. Trump has announced plans to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court.

related_stories.title: Senate Approves Bipartisan Sanctions Bill Targeting Russia and Iran
related_stories.summary: The Senate has passed a bipartisan sanctions bill aimed at Russia and Iran, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham. The legislation, which received overwhelming support with a vote of 86-11, seeks to penalize countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas, aiming to reduce revenue for the Russian government amid ongoing conflicts.
